notes.bp: A translation or spoken answer can sound similar to a source while quietly changing or contradicting its meaning.
notes.wh: Similarity rewards shared words or embeddings but does not distinguish agreement, contradiction, and unrelated content.
notes.naive: Score overlap and call a high similarity score faithful.
notes.ap: Classify the logical relation between speech and text or between two speech segments as entailment, contradiction, or neutral across languages and modalities.
notes.mech: Speech-text, text-speech, and speech-speech pairs are added to a multilingual inference framework and compared with similarity-based BLASER evaluation.
notes.math: The target is a three-way relation, not a continuous closeness score; F1 measures whether the evaluator detects meaning-preserving and meaning-changing pairs.
notes.ww: The paper reports F1 gains of 0.19 for speech-speech and 0.13 for speech-text over BLASER in distinguishing entailment from non-entailment.
notes.limits: Languages, pair construction, translations, labels, and evaluation sets bound the result; logical classification does not guarantee complete translation assessment or human usefulness.
notes.title: Beyond Similarity Scoring: Detecting Entailment and Contradiction in Multilingual and Multimodal Contexts

notes.bp: A summary of a long spoken presentation must retain the important points without forcing a model to search the whole sequence and compose everything at once.
notes.wh: Long speech contains many irrelevant stretches, and an abstractive system can lose key content while generating fluent text.
notes.naive: Generate the summary directly and assume the generator will discover the important spans.
notes.ap: First identify useful excerpts from the speech, then use that auxiliary selection signal to guide abstractive summary generation.
notes.mech: An extractive-abstractive model is trained on a web-presentation corpus, with an extractive summary predicted from raw speech alongside the final text summary.
notes.math: Selection narrows the content problem before wording is generated; METEOR compares the final summary with reference summaries while the extractive task supplies structure.
notes.ww: The method gives consistent gains and up to 1.4 METEOR points over a strong abstractive baseline.
notes.limits: The corpus, reference summaries, metric, summary length, and presentation style bound the result; lexical overlap does not prove that all important facts were preserved.
notes.title: Pick and Summarize: Integrating Extractive and Abstractive Speech Summarization

notes.bp: Wearable child recordings produce enormous naturalistic audio, but researchers need reliable labels such as who or what kind of voice appears before studying development.
notes.wh: In-the-wild recordings are noisy, imbalanced, difficult to share, and unlike curated speech data, so a better model may not solve the real bottleneck.
notes.naive: Keep changing the architecture and features until the classifier improves, while ignoring the data collection and permission process.
notes.ap: Treat data relevance, quantity, label quality, and permission to share as first-class parts of the recognition problem.
notes.mech: Three years of voice-type classification experiments on child-worn recordings compare representation features, architectures, and parameter search against data changes.
notes.math: Performance is limited by the relationship between labels and the recording environment; classification scores reveal whether engineering changes matter relative to data coverage.
notes.ww: Model and tuning improvements produce marginal gains, while more relevant and larger shareable data produce more progress.
notes.limits: The child-wearable setting, label scheme, permissions, and task definition bound the result; conclusions do not automatically transfer to adult or laboratory speech.
notes.title: Challenges in Automated Processing of Speech from Child Wearables:  The Case of Voice Type Classifier

notes.bp: A speech classifier can be made to behave normally on ordinary inputs while an attacker causes a chosen label when a hidden manipulation is present.
notes.wh: A visible poisoned sound is easy to notice, but an attack hidden inside a learned representation can preserve apparent audio quality.
notes.naive: Assume clean-sounding audio means the classifier is safe, or search only for obvious waveform triggers.
notes.ap: Rearrange latent representations inside a pretrained speech generator so the attack changes the target label while remaining hard to hear.
notes.mech: LRBA uses the normalizing flow in VITS to create rearranged utterances and poisons a small fraction of training data for speech classification.
notes.math: The attack separates perceptual quality from decision integrity; attack success rate, poisoning rate, and mean-opinion score test the tradeoff.
notes.ww: The paper reports high attack success at a low poisoning rate while retaining high perceived quality and outperforming prior attacks in stealthiness.
notes.limits: The VITS model, classifier, target labels, poisoning setup, and listener measure bound the threat; this is an attack demonstration, not evidence that every speech system is vulnerable.
notes.title: LRBA: Stealthy Backdoor Attacks on Speech Classification via Latent Rearrangement in VITS

notes.bp: A person who cannot reliably speak may still communicate through brain signals, but imagined speech produces weaker and less direct evidence than spoken speech.
notes.wh: EEG is noisy and varies across imagined, intended, and spoken modes; a model trained on one mode may discard useful shared structure or use too many channels.
notes.naive: Train separate decoders for each mode using every available EEG channel.
notes.ap: Train one model across modes with dynamic masking, then use its learned channel relevance to make a smaller single-mode decoder.
notes.mech: A joint EEG decoder covers imagined, intended, and spoken speech and is evaluated on four-vowel classification, including a channel-selection transfer step.
notes.math: Shared and mode-specific evidence are balanced by masking; vowel accuracy tests decoding while selected-channel performance tests whether the joint model identifies useful measurements.
notes.ww: Imagined-speech accuracy rises to 34.95% from a 29.18% baseline, and channel-selected single-mode models outperform models using all channels.
notes.limits: The four-vowel task, participants, EEG hardware, mode definitions, and accuracy metric bound the result; it does not demonstrate unrestricted communication or clinical readiness.
notes.title: EEG-based Speech Decoding Based on Multi-mode Joint Modeling

notes.bp: Emotion can be expressed simultaneously by words, voice melody, and a face, and a listener must decide what to do when those channels disagree.
notes.wh: Older and younger listeners may rely on channels differently, so a single average emotion score hides both channel priorities and conflict resolution.
notes.naive: Combine all channels as if they were equally reliable or measure each channel in isolation.
notes.ap: Use a cross-channel conflict task that directs attention to one channel while manipulating congruence in the others, then compare age groups and channel effects.
notes.mech: Younger and older adults perform an audiovisual face-prosody-semantics Stroop task with happy and sad cues under congruent and incongruent conditions.
notes.math: Reaction or accuracy differences reveal selective attention and integration costs; congruence tests whether one channel can override another.
notes.ww: Older adults show reduced emotion integration, especially for prosody and other nonverbal cues, with larger age differences under incongruence.
notes.limits: The task, emotions, participant groups, language, and interpretation of Stroop costs bound the result; laboratory conflict does not directly predict everyday communication.
notes.title: Age-related changes in multisensory integration of emotions in an audiovisual face-prosody-semantics Stroop task

notes.bp: Written output from speech must include words, capitalization, and punctuation, but asking one recognizer to learn all three at once can damage the underlying word recognition.
notes.wh: Formatting decisions occur at different levels from phonetic recognition, and voice activity boundaries provide timing information that text-only decoding lacks.
notes.naive: Train directly on formatted transcripts and accept errors in both formatting and the words themselves.
notes.ap: Distill word-recognition knowledge from an unformatted teacher into a formatted student and add voice-activity cues to support boundary and formatting decisions.
notes.mech: A mixed-case end-to-end ASR student receives knowledge from a unicase teacher and voice-activity information; case-sensitive and insensitive outputs are measured.
notes.math: The system separates acoustic-to-word evidence from formatting supervision; word error and case/punctuation errors expose whether formatting harms recognition.
notes.ww: The method reports up to a 9.2% relative error reduction at comparable decoding cost.
notes.limits: Training data, formatting conventions, teacher quality, decoding budget, and reported error definitions bound the result; punctuation accuracy is not the same as transcript understanding.
notes.title: Improving End-to-end Mixed-case ASR with Knowledge Distillation and Integration of Voice Activity Cues

notes.bp: Listeners must distinguish lexical tones whose pitch contours overlap and whose categories may not behave like cleanly separated bins.
notes.wh: Pitch height, movement, duration, and phonation interact, and a continuum between tones may be heard gradually rather than categorically.
notes.naive: Assign each tone one fixed pitch contour and assume every listener makes an all-or-none category decision.
notes.ap: Measure perceptual cues for all four Changde Mandarin tones and test whether tone continua meet behavioral standards for categorical perception.
notes.mech: Production and perception data examine T1–T4 contours and T2-T3 and T2-T4 continua using tone identification and cue analyses.
notes.math: The key object is the listener's response curve across an acoustic continuum; categorical perception requires a sharp boundary and reduced cross-category sensitivity, not just different labels.
notes.ww: T1 is high-level, T2 low-rising, T3 falling rather than level, and the T2-T3 and T2-T4 continua do not meet typical categorical-perception standards.
notes.limits: The Changde variety, speakers, stimuli, cue manipulation, and category criteria bound the result; it should not be generalized to Standard Mandarin or all tonal perception.
notes.title: Tonal Perception in Changde Mandarin
